links.note: Verse 11 says the world keeps going because the rain stands unfailing (வான்நின்று உலகம் வழங்கி வருதலால்) and so rain should be understood as amrita. Verse 542 opens with the same fact, வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம், and uses it as the measure of how subjects depend on the king's sceptre. The Book of Wealth takes the rain chapter's claim as settled and builds its account of rule on it.

Verse 11 gives rain the name அமிழ்தம் because the world's life continues through it. In 1106 the lover says her shoulders must be made of amrita (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்) because his life puts out new shoots at each touch (உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப). Both verses award the word for the same reason, that the thing keeps life going, once for the whole world and once in a lover's speech about himself.

no_link_reason: The verse turns on the wordplay on துப்பு (rain makes food and is food); I found no verse elsewhere that makes this double claim, and the rain-as-sustenance links sit better on 11 and 13.

links.note: Verse 13 says that if the sky proves false (விண் பொய்ப்பின்), hunger stays and torments the world (உள்நின்று உடற்றும் பசி), sea-girt though it is. Verse 734 defines a land as one that severe hunger (உறுபசி), unending disease and destructive enemies do not reach. Read together, the first mark of a proper country in the Book of Wealth rests on something no ruler supplies, the rain of chapter 2.

Verse 14 says ploughmen will not plough with the plough (ஏரின் உழாஅர் உழவர்) when the yield of the rain-cloud shrinks. Verse 1031 says the world, however it whirls about, goes behind the plough (ஏர்ப் பின்னது உலகம்). The two make a chain: the world follows the plough, and the plough waits on the rain.

Verse 14 says ploughing stops when the rain's bounty declines. Verse 1036 says that if the ploughmen's hands fold (உழவினார் கைம்மடங்கின்), even those who say they have given up desire cannot hold their state. Verse 14 names one cause that would fold those hands, so the failure of rain reaches as far as the renouncer.

Verse 15 says it is rain that ruins (கெடுப்பதூஉம்) and rain again that stands by the ruined and lifts them (எடுப்பதூஉம்); Parimelazhagar explains that it ruins by not falling. In 1102 the lover says that for other diseases the medicine is something else, but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). The pattern of one thing being both the harm and the only remedy appears for rain and the world and, in a lover's speech, for the beloved.

Verse 16 says that unless drops fall from the sky (விசும்பின் துளிவீழின் அல்லால்) not even the tip of green grass can be seen. Verse 557 says that what lack of drops (துளியின்மை) is to the earth, the king's lack of tender regard (அளியின்மை) is to those who live under him. Verse 16 supplies the picture that 557's comparison assumes: without the king's அளி, the people are the bare ground.

Verse 211 asks what the world does for the rain-cloud in return (மாரிமாட்டு என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ உலகு) and makes it the model of duty that wants no repayment. Verse 17 says even the long sea loses its nature if the cloud, having taken from it (தடிந்து, as Parimelazhagar reads it), does not give back. On that reading the cloud is not a pure giver: it returns what it drew from the sea, and the sea suffers if it withholds. Manakkudavar takes தடிந்து as lightning flashing, and on his reading the qualification falls away.

Verse 17 pictures the cloud not giving (எழிலி தான் நல்காதாகி விடின்) and the sea itself shrinking as a result. Verse 1010 says the brief want of the renowned rich has the nature of the rain-cloud gone dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது). Both use the withholding cloud; 1010 turns it into a figure for a giver's temporary incapacity, with the suggestion that it is as general a loss and as passing.

Verse 18 says that if the sky dries up (வானம் வறக்குமேல்), festival and worship for the gods will not go on here (சிறப்பொடு பூசனை செல்லாது). Verse 560 says that if the guardian does not guard (காவலன் காவான் எனின்), the cows' yield shrinks and those of the six duties forget their book (நூல் மறப்பர்). Both say religious practice has a material precondition that can fail; chapter 2 names the rain and chapter 56 names the king.

Verse 19 says giving and austerity (தானம் தவம் இரண்டும்) will not stay in the world if the sky does not give. Verse 559 says that if the king acts with justice bent (முறைகோடி), the sky will not pour in season (ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). Chapter 2 makes virtue depend on rain; 559 makes the rain depend in turn on a human virtue, the ruler's justice, so the dependence runs both ways.

Verse 19 says austerity (தவம்) cannot last without rain. Verse 1036 gives the step in between: if the ploughmen's hands fold, those who say they have left desire have no standing (விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை). The renouncer's practice rests on the farmer's food, and the farmer's on the sky.

Verse 20 says no one's world can do without water (நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு), and that ஒழுக்கு cannot exist without the sky. Parimelazhagar takes ஒழுக்கு as the water's unbroken flow; Pope's verse rendering and Kalaignar take it as ordered conduct. Verse 542 states the first half as a given (வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம்) and sets the people's dependence on the sceptre beside it. On either reading of ஒழுக்கு, 542 treats the dependence 20 argues for as the standard case of something one cannot live without.

Verse 20 ends the chapter by saying nothing in the world, for anyone, holds without the sky. Verse 55 says that for the wife who rises worshipping her husband, it rains when she says 'rain' (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). Three chapters after rain is made the condition of everything, the rain is said to answer to one person's steadfastness.

Verse 21 says the settled view of the texts (பனுவல் துணிவு) sets the greatness of those who have renounced within their discipline (ஒழுக்கத்து நீத்தார் பெருமை) highest among excellent things. Verse 48 says the household life that keeps others on their path and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). If 48 is read as ranking the householder above the ascetic, as its plain wording allows, the two chapters give the first place to different lives; if 48 is read as praising only the householder's endurance, they do not collide.

Verse 21 rests its claim on பனுவல் துணிவு, the settled conclusion of the texts. Verse 533 uses the same appeal: that the heedless have no fame is the conclusion of authors of every school (எப்பால் நூலோர்க்கும் துணிவு). These are two places where the Kural, which usually argues from observation, cites the agreement of the books as its ground.

Verse 22 says that to state the measure of the greatness of renouncers (துறந்தார்) is like counting the dead of the world (இறந்தாரை எண்ணிக்கொண்டற்று). Verse 310 rhymes the same two words: those who exceed in anger (இறந்தார்) are like the dead, and those who have renounced anger are equal to renouncers (துறந்தார் துணை). In 22 the dead supply only a number too large to count; in 310 the same pairing sets renouncers and the dead as opposite ends, and extends the renouncer's standing to anyone who gives up anger.

Verse 23 says the greatness of those who have discerned the two (இருமை வகைதெரிந்து) and taken on அறம் here stands highest in the world; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read the two as birth and release and the அறம் as renunciation. Verse 49 says that what is called அறம் is household life (அறன் எனப்பட்டதே இல்வாழ்க்கை). On the commentators' reading of 23 the two verses attach the word அறம், and the highest standing, to different lives. Kalaignar reads 23 as choosing good over bad in general, and on that reading there is no conflict.

Verse 23, as Parimelazhagar reads it, praises above all those who take up renunciation in this birth after weighing birth against release. Verse 46 asks what one who conducts household life in the way of virtue would gain by going off on the outside path (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்). If the outside path is the ascetic's, as Pope takes it, 46 denies that the step 23 praises adds anything for a good householder.

Verse 24 says one who guards the five with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்) is a seed for the best of grounds; the goad implies the senses are elephants, as Parimelazhagar notes. Verse 126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்) protects through seven. The same claim is made in the renouncer's chapter and in the householder's chapter on restraint, with different pictures of the senses: a strong animal to be driven, and limbs to be pulled in.

Verse 24 calls the one who guards the five senses a seed (வித்து) for the ground called வரன், which Parimelazhagar takes as release. Verse 361 calls craving the seed (வித்து) that bears unceasing birth for all beings. The book uses the seed for both outcomes: restraint of the senses is sown toward release, and craving is what sprouts as rebirth.

Verse 25 says Indra, king of those in the wide sky, is witness enough (இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி) to the power of one who has quenched the five. Verse 899 says that if those of exalted vows flare up, even the வேந்தன் breaks midway and loses his kingship; Parimelazhagar reads the வேந்தன் there as Indra. On his reading 899 states outright the event that 25 only points to, a king of gods brought down by an ascetic's power.

Verse 25 speaks of the power of ஐந்தவித்தான், one who has quenched the five. Verse 6 uses the same phrase for the Lord (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) whose path of conduct gives long life to those who keep it. The renouncer of chapter 3 is described in the words chapter 1 uses for the one whose feet are to be reached.

Verse 25 offers Indra as its witness, using the word கரி. Verse 245 says those who hold to அருள் have no distress, and the wide earth where the wind moves is the witness (மல்லன்மா ஞாலங் கரி). In both verses a claim about an inner quality is supported by pointing to a single witness on a cosmic scale, the king of heaven for the ascetic's power and the whole earth for compassion.

Verse 26 says those who do what is hard to do (செயற்கரிய செய்வார்) are great and those who cannot are small. Verse 975 says those who have greatness will carry out in the proper way deeds that are hard (அருமை உடைய செயல்). Chapter 3 says it of renouncers, and Parimelazhagar takes the hard things to be restraint of the senses; chapter 98 says it of greatness in worldly life. The test of greatness is the same in both books.

Verse 26 divides people by whether they can do what is hard to do. Verse 664 says saying is easy for anyone and doing as one has said is hard (அரியவாம் சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்). The chapter on firmness in action applies the renouncer's standard to statecraft and names what is hard in a deed: carrying it out as announced.

Verse 27 says the world lies within the one who discerns the kinds of the five (ஐந்தின் வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு): taste, light, touch, sound and smell. Verse 354 says that even having gained the fivefold awareness (ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும்) is of no benefit to those without perception of the real (மெய்யுணர்வு). Verse 354 sets a limit on 27: command of the five is not the end, and without true perception it yields nothing.

Verse 27 lists the five sense objects (சுவை ஒளி ஊறு ஓசை நாற்றம்) and says the world belongs to the one who discerns them. In 1101 the lover lists the same five as acts, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும் ஐம்புலனும்), and says they are all found in this one woman (ஒண்தொடி கண்ணே உள). The same inventory serves the renouncer as a field to be understood and the lover as a field of enjoyment; the second is a speech in the moment and not a counter-teaching.

Verse 28 says the greatness of people whose word is full (நிறைமொழி மாந்தர்) is shown on earth by their மறைமொழி; Parimelazhagar explains நிறைமொழி as speech that produces its result whether spoken in grace or in anger. Verse 55 says that when the wife who worships her husband says 'rain', it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). Both give a person's word power over the world as the proof of their standing, for the renouncer through austerity and for the wife through steadfastness at home.

Verse 29 speaks of the anger (வெகுளி) of those who stand on the hill of good qualities; on Parimelazhagar's reading they are sages whose anger, though it lasts a moment, cannot be warded off by its target. Verse 310 says those who have renounced anger are the equals of renouncers (சினத்தைத் துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை), which makes freedom from anger the renouncer's mark. On Parimelazhagar's reading the book's model renouncer still gets angry, and dangerously. Kalaignar reads 29 as saying their anger does not stay even a moment, and on that reading the two verses agree.

Verse 29 puts the virtuous on a hill (குணமென்னும் குன்றேறி நின்றார்) and warns of their anger. Verse 898 calls such people hill-like (குன்றன்னார்) and says that if they think ill of someone (Parimelazhagar's reading of குன்ற மதிப்பின்), those who seemed fixed on the earth perish with their line. The Book of Wealth returns to the same figure and turns chapter 3's remark into advice for kings not to offend them.

Verse 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous (அறவோர்), because they live clothed in cool kindness toward every living being (எவ்வுயிர்க்கும் செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான்). Verse 134 says a பார்ப்பான் can relearn the Veda he forgot, but his birth is ruined when conduct declines (பிறப்பொழுக்கங் குன்றக் கெடும்). Both tie the title to how one lives: 30 by defining it through kindness, 134 by saying the birth is lost with conduct.

Verse 30 defines அந்தணர் by conduct, as those who practise kindness to all beings; Parimelazhagar applies it to renouncers. Verse 543 speaks of the book of the அந்தணர் (அந்தணர் நூல்), which Parimelazhagar takes as the Veda, and says the king's sceptre stands as the ground of it and of virtue. The word is used in 543 in its ordinary sense for a group with a scripture, so a reader should not carry 30's definition into every use of the word in the book.
